summary: TechCrunch reports that Instagram users accuse Meta of shadowbanning and over-moderating content about Palestine after Hamas' attack on Israelis and Israel's retaliation. Meta blames "bugs" and denies deliberately suppressing voices, but advocacy groups and a Meta-commissioned 2021 report point to long-standing bias, especially in Arabic content moderation. The article reviews user experiences, the history since 2021, Meta's partial reforms, and workarounds users employ.
one_line: TechCrunch examines claims that Meta's Instagram suppresses Palestinian content, arguing documented systemic moderation bias goes beyond the "bugs" the company cites.
key_facts: Meta's newsroom post, updated Oct. 18, 2023, denied deliberately suppressing voice and said policies are applied equally around the world.
Meta communications director Andy Stone said a bug affected all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts, reducing reach, and that it affected accounts equally around the globe and was fixed.
Meta also said it fixed a bug that prevented users from going live, a global issue fixed within a few hours.
A 2021 third-party report commissioned by Meta found the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation.
The report found Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content and was more likely to be erroneously removed.
Over the 13 days leading up to the 2021 ceasefire, 7amleh documented more than 500 reports of Palestinian "digital rights violations."
Arabic has over 25 dialects, and Meta has been criticized for not adequately diversifying its language resources.

Instagram users reported that Stories about Palestine got far fewer views; an Egypt-based user's Stories dropped from about 300 views to one to two, and a UK user's views returned to normal after he posted a cat photo.

Instagram's auto-translation turned Arabic "Alhamdulillah" plus "Palestinian" and a flag emoji into phrases like "Palestinian terrorists – Praise be to Allah"; Meta said it fixed a problem causing inappropriate Arabic translations and apologized.

Meta committed to changes after the 2021 report, including updating dangerous-organization keywords, disclosing government removal requests, and launching a hostile speech classifier for Hebrew content.
Jillian York of EFF said moderation of English and European languages is more comprehensive partly because the EU enforces the Digital Services Act.
Meta said it set up a "special operations center" staffed with fluent Hebrew and Arabic speakers to monitor violating content during the current escalation.
Users try workarounds such as writing "p@lestine," placing text over unrelated images like cat photos, or adding Israeli flag emojis and #istandwithisrael.
